## Map: Tensions and Form

:::fragment
:::medium
[Narrow perspectives]{.highlight} 
:::

Most maps capture the headline topics (e.g., human-in-the-loop, accountability). The positions that came up in the discussions, and required attention and analysis, rarely appear.

:::small
  *Examples rarely captured:* prompt injection feeding new documents into the knowledge base that other agents then use; trust in an agent resting on who built it; overseeing agents eroding the mental models needed to diagnose failures; etc. 
:::
:::

:::fragment
:::medium
[Generic clusters]{.highlight}
:::

Many clusters stay at a level that holds for general AI usage.

:::small
  *Generic:* "When AI agents act on their own and cause damage the accountability is unclear."\
  *Precise, same topic:* "AI agents make detection and response faster, but the person who formally stays responsible has less and less real insight, skill and control."
:::
:::

:::notes
Most maps file the Hugging Face case as "agents broke out of the sandbox". Few ask why. One map does: "LLMs trained using numerical rewards specifically optimize to circumvent rules and better conceal their 'cheating'." That is where a knowledge problem starts: how much control do guardrails provide when they sit outside the objective?

A second same-topic pair on knowledge as an attack surface:

- Generic: "Friction between the effectiveness and correctness of Knowledge agents. Risk of manipulated data and lack of control of the output."
- Precise: "Trust in the information base erodes when agents retrieve, transform and pass data on to other agents with little human inspection."

Test for every phenomenon: would the statement still be true without the eight talks? If it holds for any company, it names a topic, and the phenomenon is still missing.
:::

## Map: Mapping

:::fragment
:::medium
[Tensions not worked out]{.highlight}
:::

Many maps name a tension as a label. Which two claims contradict each other, and which knowledge problem follows, remains open.

:::small
  *Label only:* "Tension: Speed vs. Control." *Worked out, same topic:* "Diehl Aviation proposes human-in-the-loop controls and decision boundaries to govern agents, while Wilken observes that frequent approvals become a bottleneck and turn into rubber-stamping. The control of one input is the cause of failure observed by another."
:::
:::

:::fragment
:::medium
[Formal weaknesses]{.highlight}
:::

A few submissions show formal weaknesses.

:::small
  *Examples:* a mind map of one's own research interests in place of a map of perspectives; claims without a kind tag, or entries that are not claims; sources that cannot be traced.
:::
:::

:::notes
The repair for every tension: name the two claims, state why both cannot hold at once, derive the knowledge problem from exactly this contradiction.

A second worked example: "Awareness vs. behaviour (Wieland 4 ↔ SITS 2). Wieland bets on training people to recognise phishing. Yet the speaker himself said that even he cannot always tell a real website from a fake one, and SITS reports that trained people clicked more, not less. If training does not change behaviour, it is unclear what people-based controls achieve."

A cluster without a genuine contradiction is a valid finding if it is stated: "No genuine contradiction identified yet."

Formal requirements come first. A map without tagged claims or traceable sources cannot be assessed on depth and tensions.
:::

## Check-in

:::fragment
:::medium
[Weak evidence]{.highlight}
:::

Many submissions name no specific reference. Others give no sign that something like a research log exists. 

:::small
  *Example:* "I learned many new IT management terms that I had no prior knowledge of."
:::
:::

:::fragment
:::medium
[Superficial analysis]{.highlight}
:::

Some submissions only give a general retrospection or a summary of what the speakers said. Most name a new ability. Few show what triggered it and what actually changed.

:::small
  *Good example (shortened):* "In my log entry, I described how I asked why managing directors in German mid-sized companies invest so little in cyber security despite being personally liable. A fellow student answered that the available funds have to go into things like corporate strategy. This challenged my assumption that knowing about liability automatically leads to investment."
:::
:::

## Take-aways

:::incremental
- **Build your research log.** A check-in can only draw on what your log recorded.\
  Individually for the check-ins. As a team, a living document: read and write, discuss and write, reflect and write.
- **Do not outsource the thinking.** The interesting perspectives came up in the discussions and needed attention and analysis. Follow them up.\
  *Outsourcing the thinking to AI tends to produce generic, interchangeable phrasing.*
- **Plan the time.** The analytical work of reading, comparing, deciding and cutting back takes longer than the write-up.
- **Read the criteria first.** Every deliverable has its own published criteria.\
  *Check your draft against them item by item before you submit.*
:::
